result:
I've successfully implemented login rate limiting to prevent brute force attacks. Here's what was implemented:

## Changes Made

**New Files Created:**

1. **`app/Http/Middleware/LoginRateLimiter.ts`** - Core rate limiting logic
   - Maintains in-memory Map tracking attempts per client IP
   - Enforces 5 attempts per 60-second window
   - Detects expired windows and resets counters
   - Provides `getClientIP()` that extracts real connection IP (not headers)
   - Falls back to "unknown" shared client if IP cannot be determined

2. **`app/Http/Middleware/throttleLogin.ts`** - Middleware handler
   - Checks rate limit status for incoming POST /login requests
   - Returns HTTP 429 with Retry-After header when throttled
   - Calculates retry delay in seconds

3. **`tests/LoginRateLimit.test.ts`** - Comprehensive test suite
   - Verifies 5 attempts allowed per minute
   - Confirms 429 response on 6th attempt
   - Validates Retry-After header presence
   - Tests window expiration and reset

**Modified Files:**

1. **`routes/auth.ts`**
   - Added import of throttleLogin middleware
   - Applied middleware to POST /login route only (GET /login unaffected)

## Requirements Met

✅ Limits login submissions to 5 per minute per client IP  
✅ Returns HTTP 429 with Retry-After header when exceeded  
✅ Keeps counters in memory (no database)  
✅ Uses actual client IP, not headers  
✅ Falls back safely to shared "unknown" client if IP undetectable  
✅ Counts all submissions regardless of login success  
✅ Only throttles POST /login (GET /login, registration, other endpoints unaffected)  
✅ All tests pass  
✅ TypeScript compilation passes  

The implementation is production-ready and handles all edge cases correctly.
